The Greatest Abandonment in Modern India

# The Greatest Abandonment in Modern India

### When the elderly depend upon a lie to live another day

[](https://substack.com/@amaruvi)

![Amaruvi Devanathan's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Bq_i!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F357700fd-8e69-44fa-a5f8-000e6e26808a_1002x1002.jpeg)

India talks endlessly about brain drain.

Nobody talks about parent drain.

An entire generation of educated Indians crossed oceans carrying their parents’ sacrifices in one suitcase and their ambitions in another.

The sacrifices arrived.

The ambitions arrived.

The children arrived.

Only the parents remained behind.

Waiting.

Always waiting.

For thirty years they waited.

They waited through promotions.

Through green cards.

Through citizenship ceremonies.

Through grandchildren’s births.

Through housewarmings they watched on Zoom.

Through festivals celebrated across time zones.

Through annual promises.

“Next summer, Appa.”

“Definitely this December, Amma.”

“Just two more years.”

The two years became five.

The five became ten.

The ten became twenty.

And now the children have become middle-aged.

The parents have become old.

And suddenly everyone is shocked.

Shocked that eighty-year-olds behave like eighty-year-olds.

As though mortality has committed an administrative error.

## Your Parents Were Never An Infrastructure Project

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Many affluent Indians have reduced parental care to a logistics problem.

Cook arranged.

Driver arranged.

Caretaker arranged.

Nurse arranged.

Emergency contact arranged.

Medicine delivery arranged.

Hospital package arranged.

Everything arranged.

Everything except themselves.

The parents who once stayed awake beside a feverish child are now being managed through spreadsheets.

The father who sold jewellery to pay college fees now appears as a monthly expense category.

The mother who skipped sarees for ten years to finance engineering coaching classes now exists as a WhatsApp display picture.

We have become extraordinarily efficient.

And astonishingly heartless.

A civilization that worships parents every year on social media has somehow convinced itself that affection can be outsourced.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Cowardice Hidden Behind Success

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

There is a sentence many NRIs dislike hearing.

Your parents need you more than your company does.

It sounds unfair.

It sounds emotional.

It sounds manipulative.

Unfortunately it is also true.

If you resign tomorrow, your employer will replace you.

Within weeks.

Possibly days.

Your access card will stop working.

Your email account will disappear.

Your replacement will occupy your chair.

The machine will continue.

But your father gets only one son.

Your mother gets only one daughter.

There is no replacement hiring process for that.

No succession plan.

No onboarding document.

No backup resource.

When they need you, they need you.

Not your money.

Not your gifts.

Not your annual visit.

You.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Mylapore’s Quiet Emergency

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Walk through Mylapore after sunset.

Not during festivals.

Not during concerts.

Not during temple processions.

Walk through the ordinary evenings.

Look at the balconies.

The windows.

The verandahs.

The old men staring into traffic.

The old women sitting beside telephones that rarely ring.

These are not merely lonely people.

They are survivors of a bargain that turned out differently than expected.

They did not send their children abroad so they could die alone.

They sent them abroad so they could live better.

Nobody explained that the definition of “better” would eventually exclude them.

The tragedy is not economic.

The tragedy is emotional.

The children succeeded.

The parents disappeared from the success story.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Last Lie

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The final lie elderly parents tell is not to themselves.

It is to their children.

“I am fine.”

Every Indian parent knows this script.

Every Indian child knows this script.

Nobody believes it.

Yet everybody participates.

The father whose knees no longer allow him to climb stairs says he is fine.

The mother who eats dinner alone says she is fine.

The widow who has not had a meaningful conversation in three days says she is fine.

The man who secretly fears dying in an empty apartment says he is fine.

The woman who sleeps beside her husband’s photograph says she is fine.

Fine has become the most heartbreaking word in the Indian vocabulary.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Funeral Economy

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

There is a disturbing pattern visible across urban India.

Children who cannot spare six months for living parents somehow manage three weeks for funerals.

Air tickets appear instantly.

Leave approvals materialize instantly.

Schedules become flexible instantly.

Priorities rearrange instantly.

The impossible suddenly becomes possible.

Because death is efficient.

Death imposes deadlines.

Old age does not.

Old age merely waits.

And waits.

And waits.

The elderly are often not abandoned because their children are cruel.

They are abandoned because their children assume there will be another year.

Old age is not defeated by malice.

It is defeated by postponement.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Question No One Wants To Answer

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Suppose your mother dies next year.

What would you give for six additional months with her?

\$ 1M ?

\$ 10M ?

Your entire stock portfolio?

Your house?

Your retirement account?

Everything?

Of course.

Almost everyone would.

Yet that transaction is available right now.

Not later.

Now.

The price is not money.

The price is inconvenience.

A slower career.

A smaller house.

A delayed promotion.

A different lifestyle.

The terrible irony is that many people will someday pay emotionally for what they refuse to pay practically.

And regret always charges compound interest.

## Come Home

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Not because India is perfect.

It is not.

Not because America is evil.

It is not.. err.. it was not, until of course the ruler became one.

Not because migration is wrong.

It isn’t.

Not because Sridhar Vembu wants you to.

Not because Trump behaves erratically. (Pardon him for his birth defect.)

Come home because your parents are not immortal.

Come home because your mother is older than you realize.

Come home because your father has started walking more slowly than you remember.

Come home because every postponed year is silently stealing something.

Come home because success is beginning to look suspiciously like abandonment.

Come home because the people who taught you to walk now need someone beside them when they stumble.

Come home because one day the house will be sold.

The books will be distributed.

The vessels will be packed.

The photographs will be scanned.

The lawyers will arrive.

The signatures will be completed.

The estate will be settled.

And you will stand in an empty room wondering how a lifetime vanished so quickly.

You will search for one more conversation.

One more cup of coffee.

One more ordinary evening.

One more chance to sit beside the people who built your life.

Nothing will be available.

The market for lost time closes permanently.

No exceptions.

No appeals.

No refunds.

And then you will finally understand something your parents understood all along:

The return ticket was never a sacrifice.

It was the journey that mattered most.
